name: Eating disorder-adjacent restriction ('thinspo' leanness)
lead: "Thinspo" (thinspiration) leanness refers to pursuing a very thin or gaunt look through severe food restriction, often inspired by images of very thin people. In looksmaxxing discussions the stated appeal is visual: low body fat makes facial bone structure, such as a defined jawline and hollow cheeks, more visible, and gives a lean physique [3]. Wikipedia lists extreme dieting, sometimes to the point of starvation, to reach a low body-fat level among "hardmaxxing" practices [3].

Thinspiration is photographic content, often of very thin women, meant to motivate continued restriction, and it is associated with pro-ana (pro-anorexia) online communities that promote behaviours linked to anorexia nervosa [1][2]. Eating disorder organisations and medical bodies generally regard these communities as harmful, arguing that they normalise illness and discourage treatment [2]. This article documents the practice and what is reported about it; it contains no instructions.

Research on this area is about exposure to the content, not about restriction as a looksmaxxing method. Surveys and experiments summarised on Wikipedia link pro-ana site viewing with more negative body image and lower mood, and a 2024 study found that short exposure to TikTok content about women's body weight lowered body image in young women [1][2]. People affected by disordered eating can contact local eating disorder helplines and healthcare providers.

chain: Severe food restriction to cut body fat
Facial and body fat falls, making cheekbones and jawline more visible
A leaner or gaunt look (as sought); documented health and eating disorder risks
angle.text: Those who pursue this aim to look gaunt or very lean, which they believe shows bone structure more clearly. Medical groups link severe restriction with eating disorders, and the research literature focuses on the harms of related online content.

infobox: Gaunt or very lean look, visible bone structure
Associated with eating disorder risk and documented harms

paras: Pro-ana content spread through free web hosts in the late 1990s and then through blogs and social networks in the 2000s, and gained mainstream attention after a 2001 Oprah special; Yahoo removed pro-ana groups that year [2]. Thinspiration images were commonly shared in pro-ana groups in the early 2000s and 2010s, and Tumblr was especially popular for them from 2011 to 2015 [1]. On TikTok the content often appears under fitness labels such as fitspiration, weight-loss journeys, body checking and "clean" eating [1].
Platforms including Tumblr, Pinterest and Instagram announced policies against pro-ana content in 2012 with limited success, and content moved to other platforms in less recognisable formats [1][2].

Wikipedia describes looksmaxxers as checking features such as hollow cheeks and a defined jawline, and lists extreme dieting among hardmaxxing practices that also include off-label weight-loss drugs [3]. Commentators cited there argue that communities that rate appearance regardless of wellbeing can contribute to body dysmorphia, and one psychology lecturer, Jamilla Rosdahl, says young people who feel unable to control their circumstances may turn to looksmaxxing as "something they can control" [3].

A 2006 Stanford survey found over a third of eating disorder patients had visited pro-ana sites, and most of those learned new weight-loss or purging methods there; a 2007 University of South Florida survey found pro-ana viewers reported more negative body image, and experiments found brief viewing lowered mood and self-esteem in women [2]. A 2010 experiment found many women reduced calorie intake after viewing pro-ana sites [2].

Some researchers argue that the sites mainly make affected people more visible rather than causing eating disorders, and that blaming them may oversimplify complex causes; some recovery groups favour understanding over bans [2]. A 2024 study by Madison Blackburn and Rachel Hogg of 273 US women aged 18 to 28 found that watching a short stretch of TikTok content about women's body weight, including neutral videos of thin women, was associated with lower body image [1].
No studies found on severe restriction as a looksmaxxing method. Studies of exposure to pro-ana and thinspiration content are summarised above.

timeline.event: Yahoo removes pro-ana groups from Yahoo Clubs after a complaint from an eating-disorder association [2].
A Stanford survey reports that over a third of eating disorder patients had visited pro-ana sites [2].
Tumblr, Pinterest and Instagram announce policies against pro-ana content [1][2].
Blackburn and Hogg publish a study of TikTok body-weight content and body image [1].

card.summary: Extreme restriction for a gaunt look, closely tied to eating disorder content.
card.note: Associated with documented eating disorder harms; seek professional support if affected.

quick.overview:
This entry covers restrictive eating aimed at extreme leanness, sharing ground with thinspiration and pro-ana content.

Medical organisations criticise such content, and research links exposure to worse mood and body image.
quick.mechanism: It involves severe caloric restriction and appearance-comparison content; no instructional detail is given here.
quick.risks: Anorexia nervosa is reported to have among the highest mortality of psychiatric disorders.[1] Support is available through eating disorder helplines and clinicians.
